newsitem.title: BRAZIL: COFFEE--Tight supply squeezes Brazil prices higher.
newsitem.headline: COFFEE--Tight supply squeezes Brazil prices higher.

text.p: Brazilian domestic coffee prices remained high amid expectations of a lower 1997/98 harvest and roasters were clamouring for the government to raise sales of its stocks to ease tight internal supply.
Low internal supply meant that roasters were buying strictly what they needed and producers were currently limited to short-covering exporters, said Francisco Ourique, director of Flavour Coffee.
"We're just seeing small bubbles of selling once producers or cooperatives have to cash in," Ourique said.

Forward sales had dwindled since the first hints in December that a lower crop could dry up domestic liquidity. Brazil was expected to ship 600,000 to 800,000 60-kg bags in February and 400,000 to 500,000 bags in March, he said.

"Assuming that (in March) Brazil sets aside 500,000 bags for export and another one million for the internal market, another 20 percent of availability will vanish," he said. "In a couple of months the internal market and exporters will be fighting for the same bag of coffee," he warned.

Luis Hafers, vice-president of the National Coffee Council (CNC), said the problem should be solved by increasing sales of the government's coffee stocks at regular monthly auctions. "In my opinion, if more is needed, more should be sold," Hafers said.
A new coffee council joining the public and private sectors was likely to address the issue at an informal meeting in Brasilia on February 4, he said.
The government will put 200,000 60-kg bags of its stocks on sale at the next auction on Feb 5, said Banco do Brasil which holds the electronic sale.
But a spokeswoman for the National Coffee Department said there were no plans yet to raise the limit on the auctions.
David Nahum Filho, secretary-general of the Brazilian Coffee Industry Association which represents roasters, said the government should have put up at least 250,000 bags at the February auction.
"They have set aside 50,000 bags exclusively for the soluble industry and 150,000 for the domestic industry is really very little," he said.
Hafers said stocks were concentrated in the hands of a few growers and the sector was having problems repaying its debts.
The head of a cooperative grouping 3,300 growers on
Thursday said that 34 percent of growers had zero coffee, 32 percent had less than 50 bags and 1.7 percent had more than 1,000 bags, according to Hafers.
"It clearly shows that there is not a symmetry between debt and stocks," he concluded.

Meanwhile, Brazilian traders threw cold water on talk in the New York market that a former U.S. Department of Agriculture representative made a preliminary forecast of 27-million-bag Brazil coffee crop in 1997/98.
Former USDA representative Leon Yallouz told a coffee seminar in Rio de Janeiro last week that he would not publish his final crop estimate until March.
But he added that the majority of trees he inspected in October and November showed signs of good recovery from the 1994 frosts.

"I heard rumors about the forecast in December," said the head of forecasting at a major trade house. "But when somebody talked about 27 million bags, no one could confirm if it was for 1996/97 or for 1997/98. It was a rumor without foundation."
The market was working with estimates of a 1997/98 coffee crop of 18 to 23 million bags versus 25 million in 96/97, said Ourique.
((--Joelle Diderich, Sao Paulo newsroom +55 11 248 5417))
